assumptions: USD million. One-year repricing gap model; rate shock 1 percentage point applies for an entire year to balances in the first-year bucket only. Ignore timing within the bucket, volume changes and hedges.

evidence.text:
|Repricing|Within one year|After one year|
|---|---:|---:|
|Rate-sensitive assets|3200|2800|
|Rate-sensitive liabilities|4100|1900|
The scenario raises both asset and liability rates in the first-year bucket by 100 basis points; rates on the other bucket are unchanged.
No fair-value duration information or deposit beta estimates are available.

qas.question: What is the first-year repricing gap, assets minus liabilities?
qas.answer: 3,200−4,100=−900 million USD. The bank has more repricing liabilities than assets in this bucket.

qas.question: Under the stated shock, estimate the one-year net interest income change.
qas.answer: −900×.01=−9 million USD. The liability expense increase exceeds the asset income increase.

qas.question: How much incremental interest income arises on the repricing assets alone?
qas.answer: 3,200×1%=32 million USD; this is before incremental funding expense of 41.

qas.question: Does the gap estimate establish the change in economic value of equity?
qas.answer: No. Economic value requires discounted future cash flows and their rate sensitivities; this one-year earnings approximation does not measure them.

assumptions: USD million. Explicitly simplified fictional CSM bridge: new business adds CSM, stated favorable future-service changes add CSM, and release reduces it. No interest accretion, FX or other movements. Do not infer full regulatory accounting.

evidence.text: Opening contractual service margin 240; CSM from newly issued contracts 75.
Favorable change related to future service adds 15; amount released for current service 60.
Actual premium cash received 420; actual claims cash paid 260. No full insurance revenue bridge.

qas.question: Compute the closing CSM under the supplied bridge.
What percentage of opening CSM does the current-service release represent?
qas.answer: 60/240=25%. This is a diagnostic ratio using opening CSM, not a coverage-unit calculation.

qas.question: How much did CSM increase during the year?
qas.answer: Closing 270 less opening 240=30 million USD. New business and future-service changes exceeded release.

qas.question: Is the closing CSM of 270 cash available for distribution?
qas.answer: No. It is the stated accounting measure of unearned future-service profit, not a cash balance. Cash flows and distributability are separate.

assumptions: USD million. No fees or distributions besides one midyear subscription. Beginning value 100. Compute subperiod returns at the external-flow boundary; cash flow itself is not a return.

evidence.text: January 1 fund value 100; immediately before June 30 subscription value 110.
Immediately after subscription of 50, fund value is 160.
December 31 fund value 168; no subsequent flows.

qas.question: What return was earned before the subscription?
qas.answer: 110/100−1=10%. The subscription occurs after the first valuation.

qas.question: Calculate the second subperiod return excluding the subscription.
qas.answer: 168/160−1=5%. Use the post-flow 160 as the start.

qas.question: What is the linked annual time-weighted return?
qas.answer: (1.10×1.05−1)×100=15.5%. Do not treat the 50 subscription as investment gain.

qas.question: Why would 168/100−1 overstate investment performance?
qas.answer: It includes external capital of 50 in ending value. Time-weighting removes the contribution's mechanical effect.

assumptions: USD million. Hypothetical policy separates existing lease liabilities, qualifying closure provisions and future operating losses. Closure payments are not included in lease liabilities. No overlap between listed amounts.

evidence.text: Existing recognized lease liabilities of closing outlets 90.
Approved and communicated closure plan creates qualifying severance obligation 18 and contract termination obligation 7.
Management expects 12 of future operating losses before shutdown; no present obligation for those losses. No settlement occurred this year.

qas.question: Calculate the new closure provision under the stipulated recognition policy.
qas.answer: 18+7=25 million USD. The 12 future operating losses do not qualify.

qas.question: What combined recognized obligations are disclosed for the affected stores?
qas.answer: Existing lease liabilities 90 plus new separate closure provision 25=115 million USD.

qas.question: Should management add the 90 lease liability to restructuring expense as if it were newly incurred?
qas.answer: No. It is an existing recognized balance; new closure provision is 25. Expense and carrying liability are not interchangeable.

qas.question: Can the closure provision identify the exact cash paid next year?
qas.answer: No. No settlement timetable or subsequent lease payment schedule is given.

assumptions: USD per unit; volumes in millions of units; all produced units sold; fixed operating cost 40 million USD in both years. Prices and variable costs held constant.

evidence.text: Product X price 30, variable cost 18; Y price 50, variable cost 20.
No other products or costs. Contribution equals revenue less variable cost; EBIT equals contribution less fixed operating cost.

qas.question: Calculate total contribution in 2024.
qas.answer: X contributes 4×12=48; Y contributes 3×30=90. Total=138 million USD.

qas.question: What is the change in EBIT from 2024 to 2025?
qas.answer: 2025 contribution=6×12+2×30=132; EBIT falls from 98 to 92, a change of −6 million USD.

qas.question: What is the 2025 total contribution margin percentage?
qas.answer: Revenue=6×30+2×50=280; contribution 132. Margin=47.14%.

qas.question: Why did EBIT decline despite more units sold?
qas.answer: The mix shifted toward X, which earns less contribution per unit than Y. Fixed costs did not change; two extra X units in millions contributed 24, while one million fewer Y units cost 30.

assumptions: USD million and million shares. Simplified full-year if-converted EPS method; after-tax interest added to ordinary earnings, conversion shares added to weighted-average shares. No other potential shares.

evidence.text: Net income attributable to ordinary shareholders 96; weighted-average ordinary shares 40.
Convertible debt annual interest expense 8; tax rate 25%; if converted, 5 million additional shares.
Include conversion in diluted EPS only if it reduces EPS for this profitable company.

qas.question: Compute basic EPS.
qas.answer: 96/40=$2.40 per share.

qas.question: What earnings adjustment is used for the if-converted numerator?
qas.answer: After-tax interest=8×75%=6 million USD. Add it back because assumed conversion avoids debt interest.

qas.question: Calculate diluted EPS after testing whether conversion is dilutive.
qas.answer: (96+6)/(40+5)=102/45≈$2.2667, below basic EPS; include the instrument.

qas.question: Does inclusion in diluted EPS prove the bonds were actually converted?
qas.answer: No. This is a hypothetical potential-share calculation, not evidence of conversion or a change in actual shares.

assumptions: USD million. Toy price-cap formula: permitted revenue = allowed return on opening regulatory asset base + regulatory depreciation + eligible operating costs. No other adjustments or taxes.

evidence.text: Opening regulatory asset base 1,800; allowed return 7%; regulatory depreciation 90.
Eligible operating expenditure 160; actual operating expenditure 175.
Actual recognized revenue 365. No balancing-account or true-up policy is supplied.

qas.question: Compute allowed return on the opening regulatory asset base.
qas.answer: 1,800×7%=126 million USD.

qas.question: Determine permitted revenue under the stated formula.
qas.answer: 126+90+160=376 million USD. Use eligible, not actual, operating expenditure.

qas.question: What is actual operating expenditure above the allowed cost component?
qas.answer: 175−160=15 million USD. This compares cost levels, not an automatic recoverable balance.

qas.question: May the company recognize an additional 11 million receivable just because actual revenue is below permitted revenue?
qas.answer: Not established. A regulatory true-up or enforceable recovery mechanism is needed; the supplied formula alone does not establish a recognized asset.

assumptions: USD million. Toy fee rule: fee 20% of pre-fee fund value above prior high-water mark, after annual management fee. No subscriptions/distributions; high-water mark not reset downward.

evidence.text: Opening fund value 92; high-water mark from prior peak 100.
Pre-fee year-end value 114; fixed management fee 2 is deducted before performance fee.
Performance fee = 20% of positive excess above 100 after management fee. No other fees.

qas.question: Find the pre-performance-fee value after the management fee.
qas.answer: 114−2=112 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate the performance fee earned under the high-water rule.
qas.answer: Excess=112−100=12; fee=12×20%=2.4 million USD.

qas.question: Compute the ending fund value net of both fees.
Why is the performance fee not 20% of the full increase from 92 to 114?
qas.answer: The contract only charges performance fee above the previous peak, after management fee. Recovery of the prior drawdown does not generate performance fee.
